identification.bodyShape: Elongated, narrow-bodied tuna with a straight (not rounded) tail outline; more slender-bodied than bluefin tuna.
identificationTraits: Long, bright yellow second dorsal fin and anal fin, with a yellow stripe running down the side.
Finlets are bright yellow with no black edging (versus bigeye tuna's yellowish finlets edged with a fine black line).
Pectoral fins are short, thick, stiff, and blade-like, reaching only to about the base of the second dorsal fin (versus bigeye's longer, thinner, flexible pectoral fin that extends past that point).
Body outline is elongated and narrow with a straight tail, versus bigeye tuna's deeper, thicker, rounded body outline.
Fresh coloration shows a bright yellow mid-lateral band with a thin blue separation from the dark back; color fades quickly after death and should not be the only field mark relied on.
identification.coloration: Metallic dark blue on the back and upper sides, changing to yellow and then silver on the belly, with a bright yellow mid-lateral stripe.
identification.adultAppearance: A slender, straight-tailed tuna with a long, bright yellow dorsal and anal fin and unmarked yellow finlets.

similarSpecies.name: Bigeye tuna (Thunnus obesus)
similarSpecies.distinction: Bigeye tuna have finlets edged with a fine black line (yellowfin's are unmarked yellow), longer and more flexible pectoral fins extending past the second dorsal fin base, and a deeper, more rounded body outline than yellowfin's straight-tailed, elongated shape.

identification.averageAdultLength: Not resolved to a single figure in reviewed sources; see gaps.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Recreational minimum retention size is 27 in curved fork length under Atlantic HMS rules; landed sizes above that vary widely by region and season.
identification.typicalWeight: Not resolved to a single typical-weight figure in reviewed sources; see gaps.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Grows to up to about 400 lb.
identification.longevity: A comparatively short-lived tuna, with a lifespan of about 7 years.

social.byLifeStage: Young yellowfin travel in mixed schools with skipjack tuna and juvenile bigeye tuna.
social.note: A schooling pelagic species throughout its life history, not a solitary hunter.

feedingStrategy.note: An apex-level predator feeding on fish, squid, and crustaceans; peer-reviewed tagging found feeding patterns tracking the vertical migration of the deep scattering layer (roughly 40-100 m) both day and night. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

dielTendency.note: Active both day and night, with a documented diel depth shift: mean daytime depth around 74 m versus a somewhat deeper mean nighttime depth around 94 m in one tagged population, following the deep scattering layer's migration rather than resting at night.

behavior.thermalDrivenBehavior: Peer-reviewed tracking found the majority (about 71%) of horizontal movement occurring between 79-82°F (26-28°C), with a broader optimal/preferred range cited as roughly 68-84°F (20-29°C). Vertical movement becomes almost completely inhibited once water temperature drops below about 46°F (8°C), and tagged fish have dived into water as cold as about 39-41°F (4-5°C) on brief excursions -- a tolerance limit, not a preference.
behavior.currentFacing: Higher habitat suitability is associated with mesoscale current fronts and eddies, especially warm-core (anticyclonic) eddy margins, where convergence concentrates prey; one study also found seasonal use of cooler, nutrient-rich cyclonic-eddy water in summer, consistent with following productivity rather than temperature alone.
behavior.depthMovement: Spends the large majority of time (97.6% in one tagged population) above 200 m, within the surface mixed layer; briefly dives much deeper (in excess of 1,000 m in one recorded case) into water below 46°F, where vertical movement is sharply reduced.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Batch spawner (roughly once every 3 days through the season) once mature at age 2-3, releasing 1-4 million eggs per event. Western Atlantic spawning timing differs by region: May-August in the Gulf of Mexico, July-November in the southeastern Caribbean (broad ocean-basin regions, not named sites). Spawning water and any staging concentration are conservation context only and are not described as holding water.

diet.primaryNote: An apex-level pelagic predator feeding on fish, squid, and crustaceans near the top of the food chain; peer-reviewed tagging found feeding activity consistent with tracking the deep scattering layer's vertical migration both day and night. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.youngOfYear: Juveniles school with skipjack and juvenile bigeye tuna, consistent with feeding on similarly small pelagic prey.
lifeStageDiet.adult: Adults feed on fish, squid, and crustaceans, with feeding activity tracking vertically migrating prey layers.

diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity is not proof that a bait event is happening now; observed current forage still comes from a direct sighting, not from this dossier.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Yellowfin tuna presence in the western Atlantic is driven by thermal preference (roughly 79-82°F for the bulk of horizontal movement) and by mesoscale current features -- eddy margins and fronts -- that concentrate prey, more than by a fixed regional calendar. Reviewed sources establish spawning-season timing (which differs between the Gulf of Mexico and southeastern Caribbean) but do not give a sourced month-by-month presence/absence calendar for the US recreational fishery, so this dossier is marked partial.

entries.habitatClass: Offshore water at mesoscale current fronts and warm-core eddy margins within the preferred thermal band.
entries.thermalContext: Within or approaching the roughly 79-82°F band associated with the majority of horizontal movement in reviewed tracking data.
entries.conservationNote: Gulf of Mexico spawning season (May-August per NOAA) is underway; spawning water is excluded from holding-water guidance.
invalidators: Assuming a fixed regional arrival date; a sourced calendar for this was not found.

entries.habitatClass: Offshore water at current fronts and eddy margins; one peer-reviewed study found seasonal use of cooler, nutrient-rich cyclonic-eddy water in summer alongside the warm-core eddy association.
entries.presentationImplication: Chum-established drift and live-bait slow troll at a located current seam or temperature break; trolling spread to search open water between features.
entries.conservationNote: Gulf of Mexico spawning season continues (through August per NOAA); southeastern Caribbean spawning begins in July. Spawning water is excluded from holding-water guidance.
invalidators: Treating a single day's surface activity as proof of sustained local abundance.

entries.habitatClass: Offshore water at current fronts and eddy margins within the active thermal band.
entries.conservationNote: Southeastern Caribbean spawning continues into November per NOAA; spawning water is excluded from holding-water guidance.
invalidators: Assuming continued Gulf of Mexico spawning-related aggregation after the May-August window without a supporting source.
